# Customer Experience is the Business

Noor Eldeen Abu Dager

Regional Automotive Executive | GM • COO • Sales & Aftersales Leader | Toyota, Lexus, Dongfeng, Forthing , MG & JAC | Middle East

2w

- Report this post

The Customer Has Become More Powerful Than Ever. The automotive industry has entered a new era. An era where customers are no longer dependent on dealerships for information. Today’s customer arrives armed with knowledge. They have already watched the videos. Read the reviews. Compared the competitors. Studied the common failures. Joined owner communities. And spoken with people who have already experienced your product. In many cases, the customer sitting across the desk knows more about a vehicle’s strengths and weaknesses than the person selling it. This changes everything. The old approach of hiding problems, delaying solutions, or relying on marketing promises is becoming increasingly ineffective. Because every customer now has a voice. And that voice can reach thousands. A single positive experience can strengthen a brand. A single negative experience can damage years of hard work. The companies winning today are not necessarily the ones with the biggest advertising budgets. They are the ones that listen faster, respond better, and build trust every single day. After more than two decades in the automotive industry, I firmly believe that customer experience is no longer a department. It is the business itself. The question is no longer: “How do we sell more vehicles?” The real question is: “How do we create customers who willingly become advocates for our brand?” What are your thoughts? Has customer influence reached its highest level in automotive history?#CustomerExperience#Aftersales#AutomotiveIndustry#Leadership#DealerOperations#ServiceExcellence#AutomotiveManagement#MiddleEast#GCC#SaudiArabia#UAE#Qatar#Bahrain#Oman#CustomerService

The challenge today is no longer access to information. Customers are connected through WhatsApp groups, owner communities, forums, reviews, and social media platforms where experiences spread faster than ever before. Every unresolved issue, delayed response, or broken promise can reach hundreds of potential customers within hours. That is why listening carefully, responding quickly, and continuously improving customer satisfaction are no longer optional—they are business necessities. In today’s market, if you are not actively managing customer trust and customer feedback, you are effectively gambling with your reputation.

Bringing quantum technologies closer to future mobility — Toyota Central R&D Labs. and KEK launch a joint research program Quantum technologies, including quantum computing, quantum sensing, and quantum communication, are opening new possibilities for problems that are difficult to address with conventional computing and measurement technologies. At the same time, turning quantum technologies into practical tools for society and industry still requires major progress. We need ways to control quantum phenomena reliably, evaluate their performance in real-world environments, and design systems that can operate with stability and reproducibility. Toyota Central R&D Labs., Inc. and the High Energy Accelerator Research Organization (KEK) have established the “Toyota Central R&D Labs.–KEK Quantum Innovation Joint Research Program.” The goal is to build foundational technologies for evaluating, analyzing, and designing quantum technologies for future mobility applications. Toyota Central R&D Labs. has been advancing applied research in areas such as quantum computing and quantum sensing, with an eye toward social implementation. KEK brings world-class expertise in accelerator science, quantum beam control, precision measurement, and technologies for extreme environments. What makes this collaboration important is that it is not a one-way transfer of knowledge from academia to industry. Researchers from both organizations will jointly define and pursue research themes as equal partners. The program will focus on topics such as understanding electron spin behavior, which is fundamental to quantum sensors and quantum computers, and developing efficient, highly reliable cooling technologies for the cryogenic environments required by quantum devices. It will also contribute to talent development in the quantum technology field by involving students and postdoctoral researchers. This is the first joint research program of its kind established by KEK. Through this initiative, the two organizations aim to connect fundamental quantum science, industrial application, and human resource development — helping build a new science and technology foundation for future mobility. https://lnkd.in/gDG9-9Hp

One thing I've learned over the years is that culture is usually easier to recognise than it is to define. You see it in small moments. How people react when things go wrong. Whether colleagues help each other without being asked. Whether someone feels comfortable suggesting a new idea. Or, in this case, whether twelve people decide to spend time preparing for a marathon together. Reading about Epson's first team at the Riga Marathon made me smile because it felt like one of those moments. Not because of the running itself, but because of what sits behind it — initiative, encouragement, commitment, and a sense of belonging. Those qualities matter on a marathon course, and they matter in business too. Thank you to everyone who represented Epson in Riga. More importantly, thank you for reminding us that culture is something people create together every day.

AI ingestion pipelines take ownership of data, but they forget to keep the paperwork. Here is what happens. The document goes in. The content stays. The governance rules get left behind. The classification label, the RBAC assignment, the acceptable use flag, the retention rule live in a layer that specified who was allowed to know what this document contains. None of those rules follow the data in. The AI process was not built to carry this metadata forward. It only cares about extracting and encoding what the document says. The gap between what your data control systems enforce and what your AI deployment can retain isn't a configuration error. It's important paperwork AI doesn't know to keep. The result is not exfiltration. No data moved. No DLP rule fired. No policy was technically violated. Instead, the access barrier just dissolved. A user querying the model can surface synthesized output drawn from documents they were never granted access to. The stack has no record of the event because the stack was watching for a different kind of event. This is the monitoring gap that makes the failure mode hard to see. DLP was built to detect movement. RBAC enforces at the source. Neither tool has a sensor at the point of ingestion where the governance layer is stripped. The governance gap underneath the monitoring gap is harder. IT governs the pipeline. Security governs the data layer. Legal wrote the acceptable use policy. Predicting how single cells respond to drugs faces two obstacles. Single-cell RNA sequencing destroys each cell it measures, so treated and untreated cells cannot be matched one to one, and responses must be compared as distributions rather than as paired cells. Separately, most methods cannot predict the response to a drug absent from the training data, the setting that matters most for drug discovery. Optimal transport can map one cell-state distribution onto another, and methods such as CellOT have applied it to perturbation modelling. These solvers are unconditional: each drug or dose needs its own model, so none can generalize to a new condition. Driessen et al., in Nature Machine Intelligence, introduce the Conditional Monge Gap (CMonge), which conditions a single transport map on arbitrary covariates. 🧬 Key results 1️⃣ A single conditional map instead of per-condition models: CMonge builds on the Monge Gap to learn one global transport map conditioned on drug, dose, or their combinations, rather than fitting a separate model for each condition. Learning the map directly avoids the training instability of input-convex neural network solvers. 2️⃣ One model performs comparably to per-condition models: On the SciPlex3 dataset of three human cancer cell lines, a single CMonge model conditioned on drug and dose performed comparably to condition-specific models trained one per drug–dose pair. The strongest dose, 10,000 nM, was the hardest to predict. 3️⃣ Unseen drugs predicted from chemical structure alone: On the full SciPlex panel of 187 drugs, holding out nine drugs at a time, CMonge generalized to unseen drugs using only RDKit molecular fingerprints. It outperformed chemCPA at the strongest dose (R² 0.78 versus 0.76), with a wider margin on metrics that capture distributional heterogeneity. 4️⃣ Heterogeneity captured at a fraction of the parameters: chemCPA tends to capture the average response, often producing collapsed predictions, whereas CMonge preserves the spread and heterogeneity of perturbed cells (MMD 0.020 versus 0.195). CMonge uses 23,000 to 580,000 parameters, against roughly 1.37 million for chemCPA and over 100 million for single-cell foundation models. The formulation is independent of the condition type, so it could incorporate covariates such as cell type or time; the authors report a parallel application to CAR-T cell designs. JGB Curve: From Steepening to Bull Flattening? The U.S.–Iran agreement can be interpreted as a downward catalyst for long-term JGB yields, with the yield curve showing signs of shifting towards a more neutral or modest bull flattening bias. Risks associated with prolonged Middle East tensions—including sustained energy subsidies weighing on fiscal dynamics, global inflation pressures, and concerns that the Bank of Japan (BOJ) could fall behind the curve—may begin to ease. In this context, some compression in fiscal risk premia at the long and ultra-long end, together with a gradual normalisation of terminal rate expectations, could contribute to a softer tone across the curve, potentially extending into shorter maturities. For shorter tenors, which are more sensitive to BOJ policy expectations, the implications are less clear-cut. While reduced supply-side risks may alleviate downside risks to growth—arguably making near-term rate adjustments somewhat easier to justify—stabilising energy prices could also point to more moderate inflation dynamics, potentially capping the medium-term terminal rate. As such, the likelihood of additional policy adjustments and the eventual level of rates may not necessarily move in tandem. With the 2y1y OIS already approaching ~2%, a meaningful portion of the anticipated tightening path appears to be reflected in pricing. In a lower-risk environment, further upside in rate expectations could therefore prove more limited, with any adjustment more likely to come through a partial unwinding of prior positioning. Nevertheless, the scope for bull flattening is not unbounded. Several factors could provide a floor for long-end yields, including uncertainty around the implementation of the U.S.–Iran agreement, persistent near-term BOJ tightening expectations, (still) elevated oil prices, and the risk that energy-driven inflation effects extend into late 2026. In addition, domestic fiscal expansion—through measures such as consumption tax cuts, increased defence spending, and growth initiatives—could sustain upward pressure on long-term yields.#Japan#JGB

One of the practical challenges in TDD massive MIMO systems is channel aging when channel information becomes outdated, reducing the effectiveness of downlink beamforming. This paper proposes a dynamic beamforming technique exploiting unified channel estimation obtained from uplink demodulation reference signal (UL-DMRS) and sounding reference signal (SRS). My dear NEC Corporation, 🙂❤️ I spent several hours researching NEC's biometric ecosystem, and the scale is far larger than most people realize. NEC biometric systems are deployed across 700+ systems in 70+ countries, support approximately 300 airports worldwide, and are involved in identity programs covering more than 1.3 billion people. Their platforms can search databases containing up to 100 million individuals in real time while achieving extraordinary levels of accuracy. Most people think biometrics means facial recognition. The reality is much broader. NEC's platforms support seven major biometric modalities: • Facial Recognition • Iris Recognition • Fingerprint & Palmprint • Finger Vein Authentication • Voice Recognition • Ear Acoustic Authentication • Gait Analysis One of the most fascinating technologies is Ear Acoustic Authentication. A wearable device sends sound waves into the ear canal and measures the reflected acoustic pattern. Because every person's ear canal structure is unique, it can be used as a biometric identifier. After initial authentication, the system can continue verifying identity using inaudible high-frequency signals in the background. What happens to the data? The answer depends on the deployment model. Traditional systems store encrypted biometric templates. Newer privacy-preserving systems can convert biometric characteristics into cryptographic keys without storing facial images or biometric templates. If a key is compromised, it can be revoked and regenerated. Some architectures process everything locally on the device, ensuring biometric data never leaves the hardware. The most important takeaway: NEC typically does not own the biometric data. The organization deploying the system an airport, government agency, bank, enterprise is usually the data controller. NEC acts as the technology provider and processor operating under contractual instructions. Today, NEC technology powers airport operations, border control systems, law enforcement platforms, national identity programs, banking authentication, healthcare systems, stadium access, and enterprise security solutions across the globe. This creates one of the most interesting paradoxes in modern technology. The same company offers privacy-preserving authentication systems that store no biometric data while also enabling large-scale identity systems serving governments, airports, and organizations worldwide. # Tumor-resident T cells and dendritic cells in melanoma immunotherapy response

LifeAnalytics - CEO, Founder | Developer of Image Analysis, Flowcytometry, genomics, mass spectrometry, and molecular structure analysis software | Global Business Development | 29k+ Followers

1w

In cancer immunotherapy, it is becoming increasingly clear that the presence of immune cells alone is not enough. We also need to understand where these cells are located within the tumor and how they interact with neighboring immune and stromal cells. Today’s paper focuses on melanoma and investigates how the spatial organization of the tumor microenvironment is associated with response to immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy. The authors performed spatial and single-cell profiling of 32 metastatic melanoma lymph node samples, including treatment-naïve, ICI-resistant, and ICI-responsive cases. One of the most interesting findings is that tumor areas from ICI responders were enriched for both CD8+ and CD4+ tumor-resident T cells. CD8+ tumor-resident T cells were clonally expanded, and both CD8+ and CD4+ tumor-resident T cells showed increased expression of cytotoxicity-related genes, suggesting active anti-tumor immunity. In contrast, ICI-resistant tumors showed chronic IFN-γ response pathways associated with T cell exhaustion. The key highlight of this study is the identification of a spatially organized immune triad composed of CD8+ tumor-resident T cells, CD4+ tumor-resident T cells, and type-3 dendritic cells (DC3) that was specific to responding tumors. This work highlights that successful immunotherapy may depend not only on which immune cells are present, but also on how they are spatially organized within the tumor microenvironment. Spatial biology, single-cell profiling, and pathology-based tissue analysis will likely become increasingly important for predicting immunotherapy response, identifying biomarkers, and understanding mechanisms of therapeutic resistance. It provides a masterclass on how autonomous AI is shifting the very paradigm of financial transactions and gatekeeping. Here is my concise summary of the core concepts and strategic implications: 1. From "Instructions" to "Mandates." The Shift: Payments will move from explicit, human-driven "instructions" to agent-mediated decision-making based on pre-defined "mandates". The Architecture: The paper introduces a 3-layer framework: (1) Intent & Orchestration, (2) Authorization & Control, and (3) Settlement. The Boundary: AI operates at the upstream (intent formation), while the downstream (authorization/settlement) remains deterministic and rule-based. This ensures legal certainty and payment finality. 2. The Advent of "Agentic Compliance." Real-Time & Embedded: AML/CFT will evolve from retrospective, batch-based screening into real-time, embedded compliance. The Multi-Agent Ecosystem: We are entering a two-tiered architecture where the Remitter's Agent (optimizing FX, routing, and liquidity) interacts directly with the Financial Institution's Agent (handling real-time risk scoring, sanctions screening, and liquidity management). 3. The Evolving Role of the Gatekeeper Beyond KYC to KYA: Financial institutions' roles as gatekeepers will not shrink; they will become more dynamic. Dynamic Governance: The focus shifts from merely verifying a customer's static instructions to continuously validating the agent's behavior against its delegated mandate. Compliance will evolve from static checks to a framework integrated with KYA (Know Your Agent), mandate traceability, and automated risk scoring. As we close our Microsoft fiscal year 2026 this week I’m taking a moment to reflect. I’m grateful for the experiences I gained driving enabling operations and the learnings I’ve been able to apply as the Global Lead for our CASA team. Earlier this month, I had the pleasure of attending the Fortune COO Summit as bookend to that experience and I was invited share my perspective on “Why COOs are so uniquely placed to lead”. Microsoft Small and Medium Business organization is focused on serving the millions of Small and Medium Enterprises that make up the backbone of our global economies and communities. In my role as GSMB COO, I dealt with the challenges of ‘doing more with less’, re-designing workflows and job scopes, and pushing the frontier on our capabilities. While COO roles look different in different contexts, I believe we have a few things in common: - A bias to action. We run toward the problem and we try to get close enough to the bare metal to understand and address root-causes. - An expansive curiosity. We’re curious enough to ask ‘why?’ and to seek an end-to-end perspective. We know that addressing a pain point in isolation drives incremental impact, but addressing a cascading chain unlocks exponential impact. - We make it happen. We have a true ownership mindset and we are focused on delivering for our stakeholders and customers. At CASA we work with the leaders of many of the world’s most technically-intensive SMBs to build GIANT futures on Microsoft’s platforms. C-suites of today and tomorrow need the execution chops to translate strategy into action, progress, and impacts in faster and faster cycles. The vision to re-imagine and re-architect to build durable new capabilities and advantages. And the tech-fluency to understand how choices across data & platforms, systems & workflows, and governance & risk all come together to turn technology into leverage. Fiona Fung has been an engineer for 25 years - IBM, Microsoft's Visual Studio, Facebook Marketplace, and now the teams behind Claude Code and Cowork at Anthropic. So when she talks about engineers and AI, she's not lecturing from the sidelines. She's lived through every abstraction shift there is, and she talks about it with real warmth and curiosity. One of her former managers started out writing software on 𝘱𝘶𝘯𝘤𝘩𝘤𝘢𝘳𝘥𝘴. Today he messages her constantly about what he's building with Claude Code. What a reminder that curiosity doesn't have an expiration date. So many seasoned folks are diving in headfirst (even in retirement), and it's genuinely fun to watch. I've seen the flip side with friends, too. They tried an early model, watched it stumble, and quietly filed AI under "not good enough." Totally understandable. But the curve is exponential. The thing that didn't work three months ago is often worth another look, because the next model just made it possible. The opportunity is in staying curious instead of judging the whole space by one moment in time. As Lenny Rachitsky framed it, this is the next level of abstraction - the same jump as binary to assembly to high-level code. It keeps climbing, and now prompts are the layer we work at. AI isn't a break from how software has always evolved, it's another rung on a very old ladder. So what's next for engineers? Less typing, more judgment - verification, taste, product sense, and the freedom to ask bigger questions now that coding isn't the bottleneck. The ceiling just lifted. The fun part is deciding how ambitious you want to be. 💪

Imagine being told you were free... ...and then waiting more than two years to hear the news. That's the story of Juneteenth. On June 19, 1865, Union troops arrived in Galveston, Texas, and announced that enslaved African Americans were free—more than two years after the Emancipation Proclamation had been issued. Think about that. Freedom had already been declared. But until truth arrived, until people acted, and until justice was enforced, countless lives remained unchanged. That's why Juneteenth is more than a date on the calendar. It's a reminder that progress is not always immediate.That justice can be delayed.And that hope can endure even in the darkest moments. As Martin Luther King Jr. said: "The arc of the moral universe is long, but it bends toward justice." That bend doesn't happen on its own. It happens because people choose courage over fear.Hope over despair.Unity over division. Today, we honor those who endured, those who fought, and those who never stopped believing in a free tomorrow. May we continue their work by creating more opportunity, extending more compassion, and leaving the world more just than we found it. Build the Culture You Believe In Culture is not a mission statement on a wall. It's not a slogan, a company event, or a set of values written in an employee handbook. Culture is what employees experience every day. It's how people are treated when they succeed. It's how they're supported when they struggle. It's how leaders communicate, make decisions, and demonstrate respect for the people who help drive the organization forward. As leaders, we have a responsibility to intentionally build the culture we believe in—not simply accept the culture that develops by default. For me, this has always been one of the most important aspects of leadership and one of the reasons I genuinely enjoy what I do. I take great pride in creating environments where employees feel supported, valued, respected, and empowered to succeed. I believe in a culture where people are encouraged to grow professionally and personally. A culture where leaders listen, communicate openly, and recognize that employees are more than just a job title or a number on a spreadsheet. The strongest organizations understand that their greatest asset is their people. When employees know they are appreciated, supported, and empowered to succeed, engagement increases, retention improves, and teams perform at a higher level. Culture doesn't happen by accident. It is built through consistent actions, meaningful relationships, and a genuine commitment to investing in people. At the end of the day, employees may forget policies and procedures, but they will always remember how their workplace made them feel. Build the culture you believe in, invest in your people, and the right people will want to be a part of it.

# Stablecoins Solve Real Problems for Emerging Markets

Innovation Experience Research & Strategy @ Mastercard | Empowering Mid-Senior Level Women In Tech @ HerSynergy

4d

- Report this post

Stablecoins are not just a trend. They are one of the most practical financial tools I’ve experienced firsthand. When I moved back to Nigeria from the US in 2018, I was working remotely and earning in USD, which was great but accessing those dollars was another story. My US bank considered Nigeria a high-risk location, so accessing my account often meant waiting for US business hours, calling customer support, and repeatedly verifying my identity. It was frustrating, but it still felt better than holding naira while it rapidly lost value. In 2021, I joined a crypto company and started getting paid in stablecoins instead. While this removed the traditional banking friction, it introduced a new kind of challenge: poor product UX and unreliable P2P off-ramps. I often had to wait hours to convert funds, and sometimes deal with failed transfers and customer support issues. Still, stablecoins were better because they gave me a way to hold stronger currency which in many ways, gave me more financial freedom than traditional banking could. That's why I think a lot of conversations about stablecoins miss the point: the utility isn't new. For millions of people across Africa, Latin America, and other emerging markets, stablecoins are not interesting because they are crypto. They matter because they solve real problems around saving, moving, and accessing money. Regulation will keep evolving, and that matters. But I suspect regulation will have to catch up with a reality that already exists: when people find a better way to preserve value and move money, they use it. I'm equally bullish on Africa's role in the future of payments. We've spent decades leapfrogging legacy systems, and I believe the next wave of payment innovation will emerge not just from Silicon Valley, but from cities like Lagos, Cairo, Nairobi, and Johannesburg. My co-authors, Iwalola, Lade, and I explore this and more in our book on designing usable products for African users (waitlist link in the comments).

⚡ The biggest AI mistake in 2026 is starting with the model. Everyone wants to know which LLM to use. Whether to fine-tune. Whether agents are ready. Whether to build on GPT or Claude or something open source. None of that is the actual question. The actual question is 👉 : which process in your business is broken, repetitive, or slow enough that a human shouldn't be doing it anymore? Start there. Map the workflow. Understand where decisions get made, where data is missing, where handoffs fail. Then figure out whether AI belongs in it at all. Most of the time, the answer is yes. ✅ But the AI ends up looking nothing like what the team originally imagined, because the original imagination started with a model capability instead of an operational need. We've seen teams spend three months evaluating models for a use case that turned out to need a better database schema first. 🔻 Pick the process. 🔻 Then pick the tool. The model is the last decision, not the first.

I recently met with a biotech leadership team navigating a challenge that’s becoming increasingly common across the industry. The science was strong, the clinical data compelling, and the program was advancing quickly -- but many of the manufacturing and commercialization questions that could significantly impact the program later were still being evaluated in parallel. How would the process scale through clinical development? Would the manufacturing approach still support the needs of the program as it evolved? Did the process enable timelines to be accelerated? Would the existing strategy support long-term supply continuity and commercialization readiness? What the conversation reinforced for me is how important it has become to evaluate these CMC considerations earlier, particularly as biologics programs grow more complex and development timelines remain under pressure. These are the kinds of discussions shaping continued investment across our biologics development and manufacturing network at Thermo Fisher -- from infrastructure designed to help accelerate path-to-First In Human timelines to expanded sterile manufacturing and commercial-scale biologics capabilities to support programs as they move toward later-stage development and commercialization. Most data transformations fail for reasons that have nothing to do with the stack. That was the throughline of my conversation with Shachar Meir- former Director of Data Engineering at Meta, former data lead at PayPal- on the new episode of Data Splash. After 20+ years in data, his diagnosis is that the root cause is almost always people, process, or culture. The "missing ingredients," as he calls them. And his advice to data leaders is counterintuitive: the worst thing you can do is announce a big modernization project. A successful migration just does the same things on a new platform. The business doesn't see it and doesn't care. Deliver value first; change the technology underneath it incrementally. We also got into AI, where Shachar is refreshingly un-hyped. He sees it as the next step in a decades-long shift from telling computers how to do something to telling them what we want but he's not convinced it makes data engineering obsolete. His analogy: a modern phone gives you a better camera than professionals had 40 years ago, and you still hire a photographer for the event that matters. Enablement isn't the same as expertise. The one thing he's certain about: understanding the business has never mattered more than it does right now. If you lead a data team, or are early in your data career and trying to figure out where this is all going, this one's worth 23 minutes. Link to full episode in comment below.

ECHO (Environment Cross-entropy Hybrid Objective) demo support just landed in OpenEnv, and it's a cool idea: train agents to learn a world model almost for free Original paper by Vaish Shrivastava, Piero Kauffmann, Ahmed Awadallah, and Dimitris Papailiopoulos at Microsoft When an agent acts in an env, a rollout has 2 sides: what the agent writes and what the env writes back Normal agent RL would only train on the agent's side Train a CLI agent with GRPO and the reward shapes the action tokens, while the env's responses get masked out of the loss All that ground-truth about what actually happened gets thrown away ECHO proposes using that part too instead of discarding it On top of the usual RL loss on actions, it adds a small cross-entropy loss on the env's tokens, so the model also learns to predict what the env does L = GRPO(actions) + λ · CE(observations) And this is almost free: those tokens already passed through the same forward pass, the logits are already computed, so no extra rollout and no teacher model You get a world model as a side effect, even failed rollouts turn into signal, and the gains are real: up to 2.3x faster training and TerminalBench 2.0 pass@1 roughly doubles To learn more about the idea check out the article by one of the paper's authors (Dimitris Papailiopoulos): https://lnkd.in/eQjAWBda Concretely, OpenEnv now lets you tag, per token, what was an action vs an env observation, plus a world-model coefficient It ships with two runnable demo examples Check them out here: https://lnkd.in/eS_dKMuZ This brand new research already sits inside the open standard of OpenEnv! Additionally, check these other resources: > PI blog: https://lnkd.in/eMV5U3A9> ECHO in enterprise RL with Foundry (by Govind Kamtamneni): https://lnkd.in/esAhHwx9

Salesforce Admins are entering a new era. For years, we’ve been able to customize Salesforce with flows, page layouts, validation rules, reports, and automation. But when it came to creating truly custom front-end experiences for users, that usually meant calling in a developer, spinning up a larger project, or accepting the limits of standard Salesforce UI. That’s changing. I’ve started working on an example platform that shows what’s now possible when Salesforce Admin knowledge is combined with modern front-end tooling: fully custom interfaces built around Salesforce data, designed specifically for how users actually work. Think: - Custom dashboards that don’t feel like standard reports - Guided record experiences for specific teams - Field and object analysis tools for admins - Sales data views tailored to business processes - Cleaner, faster interfaces for users who don’t need the full Salesforce backend The exciting part is that this doesn’t replace Salesforce. It makes Salesforce more usable. The CRM remains the source of truth, but the user experience can be shaped around the business instead of forcing every team into the same standard screens. For clients, this opens up a powerful middle ground: more flexible than standard Salesforce configuration, lighter than a full enterprise app build, and focused on solving real workflow problems. I’m building this out as a practical example of what Salesforce teams can achieve when they stop thinking only in terms of “what can we configure?” and start asking “what experience should our users actually have?” If your Salesforce users are fighting the interface more than using the data, there may be a much better way to support them. This year's intern class includes Olympians, elite athletes, accomplished musicians, and nonprofit founders, not just candidates with perfect GPAs and polished technical skills. The question isn't whether Goldman Sachs is becoming more selective than Harvard University, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, or Stanford University. The question is whether AI is redefining what talent looks like in the first place. Accenture has acquired Whalar's creator and social agency business, bringing it into Accenture Song while establishing a three-year strategic partnership with the remaining Whalar Group ecosystem. Why does a neural network output probabilities that sum to 1? The answer is the softmax function: e^{z_i} divided by the sum of e^{z_j} over all classes. This equation takes raw scores, called logits (z_i), and transforms them into a valid probability distribution. Each logit is exponentiated using Euler's number (e) to ensure positivity and to amplify differences between scores. Then, each exponentiated value is divided by the total sum of exponentiated logits across all K classes, forcing the outputs to lie between 0 and 1 and sum to exactly 1. The result, softmax(z_i), is the predicted probability for class i. This matters because it enables multi-class classification tasks, such as identifying which of 1,000 ImageNet categories an object belongs to, with interpretable confidence scores. Without softmax, raw logits can be negative or unbounded, making them meaningless as probabilities. A key property: softmax is invariant to adding a constant to all logits, but sensitive to scaling. There's a pattern I keep seeing across commerce transformations. Companies respond to structural shifts too late, and at the wrong level of the organisation. History is instructive. Consider a shift we're still processing: Mobile didn't just change how people browsed. It changed how decisions formed, how context travelled with the customer, how the boundary between momentous experience, discovery and purchase dissolved. Most companies processed that as a UX problem. (Responsive!) Then a channel problem. (App!) Then, eventually, a strategic one, by which point the window for structural advantage had already closed. Agentic commerce is the current version of this. The question isn't whether AI will change how people shop. We all know the answer: It will, and it already is. The relevant question is where in your organisation the response is happening. If it's sitting in a product team or a digital innovation unit, you're probably solving at the interface layer again. The shift that needs to happen for adaptation lies deeper: What happens to your marketing logic, your commercial architecture, your data positioning when the customer's agent (or some novel emerging construct) is involved and, to an extent, running the show? That's a cross-functional question. And here's what I've learned doing this work: The answer rarely comes from one function. It comes from product, marketing and commercial strategy _in the same room_. Not in sequence, not in separate workstreams, but simultaneously. Transformation, I have come to understand, is by definition a dynamically interactive and socially embedded process. It cannot happen from the armchair. Organisations that aren't structurally open to that kind of permeability between functions don't fail at transformation because of the wrong strategy. They fail before the strategy even gets a fair chance. When did your organisation last put product, marketing and commerce in the same room: not for a presentation, but to think? I'll be at K5 - Future Retail in Berlin on the 23rd and 24th, this is one of the conversations I'm most interested in having.#K5#Commerce#Strategy#AgenticCommerce

Planes fly high because the air gets thinner. At cruising altitude, usually around 30,000 to 40,000 feet, there is less air resistance pushing against the aircraft. That helps the plane use less fuel and move more efficiently. But there is a tradeoff. Engines still need enough oxygen to burn fuel, and wings still need enough air moving over them to create lift. So aircraft do not just climb as high as possible. They climb to a range where fuel efficiency, engine performance, weather avoidance, cabin pressure, and air traffic routes all balance out. That is why commercial jets spend most of the trip high above the clouds. Not because it looks better from the window. Because the physics is cheaper up there.

Transcript Transcript

##### Transcript

Now, it's true that one of the benefits of flying at 30,000 feet is a smoother ride. This is at the top of the troposphere, the layer in which most weather occurs, so there's less turbulence and fewer storms to navigate around. But this is not the main reason that planes fly so high. The bigger reason, of course, is money. As you go up, the density of air decreases and at 33,000 feet or 10 kilometers, the density of air is just a third of what it is at sea level. So flying at this altitude, the plane runs into a third of the air molecules it would closer to the ground. That means the plane can fly about 73% faster for the same amount of thrust, and as a result you get to your destination faster and since you spend less time in the air, you burn less fuel. Not only that, jet engines are more efficient at altitude. They work by compressing air at the intake, mixing it with fuel and igniting it. So the combustion products are ejected very fast from the exhaust nozzle.

PROJECTS DON'T DELIVER OUTCOMES - PEOPLE DO 👥 Last week I had the great pleasure of moderating a panel on project execution at Inter-American Development Bank Knowledge Week in Port of Spain alongside Ian Ho a Shu, Peter Ganesh and Jonathan Barcant. As you can see, we had a whale of a time! The conversation was refreshingly candid. What struck me most was that, despite varying perspectives from development finance, government and the private sector, we struck remarkable alignment on one key premise from the outset: The most successful projects aren't necessarily the best designed - they're the ones where engagement with implementing teams is genuine, sustained and intentional from conception through to completion. Too often we "consult" the people closest to delivery after a project has been designed, approved and procured, and then spend the next 18 months telling them what has already been decided. Then we're surprised when momentum fades, risks emerge too late, or ownership never materialises. Project delivery is ultimately a leadership challenge. The role isn't about having all the answers, but about creating regular opportunities for implementing teams to raise concerns, adapt to changing circumstances and influence decisions as the project evolves. Successful projects are delivered by engaged people. And engaged people are led—not managed. Huge thanks to Julian Belgrave, Dorri Agostini, Alix X Lewis and the team at IDB T&T Country Office for including me in this important conversation.

Five years ago this month, I moved back home to Manila. Singapore is where it all began for me. I moved there straight out of university and started my career at Unilever — and over the decade that followed, I built so much of who I am professionally. Those years gave me plenty: the chance to grow into global and regional roles, to sharpen my marketing expertise, and to work on some of the biggest and most amazing brands we have. It was a formative chapter, and one I’ll always be grateful for. Which is exactly why coming home felt like such a bold decision. It’s the kind of move that comes with a lot of unspoken assumptions: that opportunity lives elsewhere, that staying home means settling, that coming back is a step away from growth. I’ve found the opposite to be true. I won’t pretend it was a leap everyone gets to make. I was fortunate to have a company in Unilever that saw my personal decision and my professional ambitions as one and the same — and supported both. A special thank you to my boss at the time, Aseem Puri, who truly made this move possible. That’s a privilege I don’t take lightly, and one I know isn’t available to everyone who wants it. What I didn’t expect was just how much that move would reshape my path. I came back in the middle of the pandemic — flying into Manila, quarantining, doing my onboarding from a hotel room. And I came back into a part of the business I’d never worked in before: Unilever Food Solutions. Five years later, it’s become the most fulfilling chapter of my career. But the part I treasure most is simpler than any of that: being home with my family. It re-energizes me every single day, and it’s what lets me bring my best self to work. I’m growing as a marketing leader and I’m present for the people who matter most — and I’ve learned that you don’t always have to choose between the two. I woke up this morning thinking about that decision I made five years ago — and I just felt this need to put my gratitude into words. For the leap, and for everything it’s given me since. 🧡

Super congrats Monica on your great journey

GSK Isn't Building AI. It's Building a Better Understanding of Human Biology. Most companies use AI to be faster. Faster reports. Faster coding. Faster emails. Faster decisions. GSK appears to be pursuing something far more difficult. And potentially far more valuable. It is trying to understand human biology better. Because the biggest challenge in drug development is not technology. It is biology. For decades, pharma searched for more data. Today, it has more data than ever before. Genomics. Clinical trials. Medical imaging. Scientific literature. Real-world evidence. The challenge is no longer collecting information. The challenge is understanding what it means. That is where GSK's AI strategy becomes interesting. For years, GSK's purpose was simple: "Do More. Feel Better. Live Longer." Today, its mission is: "We unite science, technology and talent to get ahead of disease together." That shift tells an important story. The old purpose focused on outcomes. The new mission focuses on capability. Science. Technology. Talent. Working together to understand disease earlier, predict it better, and intervene more precisely. Now a new chapter is beginning. Now, I wonder if spice is taking that evolution one step further. Spicy margaritas seem to be earning a permanent place on cocktail menus. Then I came across Mother Root’s new Jalapeño Ginger. A few days later, while wandering around Taste of London, I spotted Picoso Drinks, a spicy soda designed as a stand alone drink and a mixe. Three different places. The same signal. As a Mexican, I couldn’t help but smile. Growing up, spice in drinks was simply part of the experience. A Tajín rim on a margarita or a beer, the unmistakable flavour of a michelada, tamarind with chilli… these weren’t trends, they were part of our culture, extended into beverages. Seeing those flavour cues interpreted in new ways, and finding their place in a broader global drinks culture, is something I find fascinating. It also made me think about something bigger: as consumers continue to explore adult drinks in new ways, both with and without alcohol, flavour is taking on a new role. Alongside functional ingredients, botanicals and fermentation, spice offers something different. It brings depth. It creates layers of flavour that evolve with every sip. It slows you down, gives you something to sip and savour, and transforms a drink from simple refreshment into a richer, more memorable experience. Perhaps that’s the bigger shift. Drinks are increasingly expected to do more than refresh. They’re expected to surprise, linger and create a moment. Lasting culture change requires more than simply encouraging employees to behave differently, according to Lloyds Banking Group chief people and places officer Sharon Doherty. Speaking at the CIPD Festival of Work on 11 June, Doherty told delegates: “If you are in the middle of a culture change and you're only focusing on [employee] behaviours, it's highly likely that your culture change won't work.” The warning follows a turbulent period for Lloyds. The bank spent years recovering from its taxpayer bailout after the 2008 financial crisis, before launching a major transformation programme in 2020. As Lloyds began its transformation journey, preserving employee trust was an important challenge, Doherty said. Doherty said organisations should not delay difficult decisions during periods of major change. “If you've got tough things to do in a big transformation, do them early, because what you can see is the impact it has on engagement,” she advised. "When we started without all of those things and many others in place, people were really happy, but we were not high performing… But by having the tough love conversations… by being fair and balanced, we built our way back up to where we were, but with a very different profile of organisation." The cultural and organisational changes made over recent years have helped prepare Lloyds for the next phase of its transformation, Doherty said – embracing artificial intelligence. The bank has moved from being ranked around 200th among the world's largest banks for AI capabilities to being among the top 15, according to Doherty. For HR leaders, Doherty said: “I do think this is a Covid moment again for us in the HR function… If we don't step up, we will absolutely be sidelined, because this is now mission critical and our businesses cannot wait for us.”

It challenged assumptions, broadened perspectives, and strengthened my understanding of strategy, leadership, and organisational behaviour. However, my experience also highlighted an uncomfortable reality. During my MBA, the vast majority of my cohort were international students, primarily from India and China. I often spoke with British students on campus and many questioned the return on investment of postgraduate education. One conversation has stayed with me. Perhaps it is whether we have spent too long treating a university degree as the only respectable pathway to success. “Data is what people who can’t spot a player use.” A provocative comment heard at a U21 game — but it misses the bigger picture. The real question isn’t data versus the eye. It’s quantity versus quality, and crucially: when do we have enough information to decide? Translating numbers into “quality” requires context, sample size, and careful interpretation. Data tells you what happened, but rarely why. Subjective judgment spots the intangibles: composure, decision-making, bravery, tactical awareness, often from just one viewing. Yet it is limited by time, bias, and scale. So where is the balance? When is enough, enough? Highly respected former Manchester United youth recruitment specialist Mark Anderson puts it best: “Eyes and ears.” That works perfectly where data is scarce — in youth football or lower leagues. Add smart analytics in senior football, and it becomes “eyes, ears, and evidence.” A recent example: When given only vague details of a player I had watched on a highlights reel — a player from Sweden’s third tier, no name, no club, no position, and just one aspect of his play that had caught my attention — MUD Analytics founder Lee Mooney quickly produced a shortlist. The player in question was on it. Data didn’t replace the eye it magnified it. It turned hours of searching into minutes, shifting the question from “Can we find him?” to “What details are worth investigating further?” This was a meeting of minds: one subjective, one objective, united by a common pursuit. The truth is that data alone doesn’t guarantee better decisions. But combined with expertise, it becomes incredibly powerful. The best analytics providers I’ve encountered repeatedly adapt their platforms for the end user, harvesting narrow, relevant sets from vast amounts of information. Not to “dumb down” insight, but to recognise an essential truth: They champion the human element. Football expertise remains central. Drowning users in a sea of numbers when they only need to get their metaphorical feet wet risks disengagement. Detail is where providers prove their worth, and “less is more” becomes a genuine value. Focused information can come in bites, not volumes. Time is finite. The best use of it in scouting and coaching remains a priority. When aligned, we act effectively, focus our energy, and uncover more possibilities. The transition from legacy MT messages to the rich, structured data of ISO 20022 is a foundational shift . Banks are seeing dramatic operational benefits, with one institution reporting a 50% reduction in AML false alerts due to better data quality . This richer data also minimizes manual repairs and investigations, significantly lowering operational costs . SWIFT gpi: Real-time tracking for better liquidity. gpi provides end-to-end payment tracking and fee transparency . This isn't just a customer convenience; it's a working capital tool. When treasurers can see precisely where funds are and when they'll arrive, they can optimize cash flow and funding strategies . For Fintechs: Data is the New Product For fintechs, these standards are the key to unlocking powerful new services and competing effectively with traditional banks. Innovation at the data layer. ISO 20022’s rich, structured data is a goldmine. Fintechs can build superior products around data enrichment, validation, and exception prevention . This data is also a perfect foundation for AI, enabling more accurate fraud detection, automated KYC processes, and real-time payment insights . Leveraging new capabilities. Fintechs can directly integrate with SWIFT's ecosystem through APIs. Services like Payment Pre-validation allow fintechs to validate payee account details before a transaction, reducing failures and cost . The "composable stack" model. The new paradigm shifts competition from owning the network to orchestrating different layers. Fintechs can focus on excelling at specific layers like distribution (e.g., Volopa) or data analytics, while leveraging SWIFT rails for settlement . AI thrives on the structured, high-quality data ISO 20022 provides, enabling predictive analytics and automated compliance. 18,961 followers

1w

The market does not need more identifiers. It needs the ones it already has to evolve and connect. That is the argument in GLEIF CEO Alexandre Kech's latest blog, written alongside his Trust Talks conversation with Laura Stanley, Director of Entity Data and Symbology at LSEG(The London Stock Exchange Group) and Vice Chair of the ANNA - Association of National Numbering Agencies Board. As digital assets move into mainstream financial infrastructure, the instinct is to treat the shift as a clean break between traditional and decentralized finance. The more realistic path is coexistence, and its cost lands downstream on the banks, issuers, and infrastructure providers who have to consume any new data field. The case is for extending what already works. Identifiers like the Legal Entity Identifier (LEI), the International Securities Identification Number (ISIN), and the Digital Token Identifier (DTI) sit at different levels of granularity. What connects them is the mapping between layers, and that mapping connects every instrument or token back to the organization behind it. An identifier is just a string of characters. Its value is the governed reference data attached to it, and knowing which legal entity stands behind a transaction does not stop mattering when the technology changes. 📚 Read the blog: https://lnkd.in/eVwnnAtb🎧 Listen to the conversation: https://lnkd.in/eWKdJ76e#GLEIF#LEI#vLEI#Interoperability

Sep 2013

Jones PW, Adamek L, Nadeau G, Banik N. The 2011 Global Initiative for Chronic Obstructive Lung Disease (GOLD) strategy document recommends assessment of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) using symptoms and future exacerbation risk, employing two score cut-points: COPD Assessment Test (CAT) score ≥10 or modified Medical Research Council dyspnoea scale (mMRC) grade ≥2. To explore the equivalence of these two symptom cut-points, the relationship between the CAT and the mMRC and St George's Respiratory Questionnaire (SGRQ), the Short-form Health Survey and the Functional Assessment of Chronic Illness Therapy Fatigue scores were retrospectively analysed using a primary care dataset. Data from 1817 patients (mean±sd forced expiratory volume in 1 s 1.6±0.6 L) showed a significant association between mMRC grades and all health status scores (ANOVA p<0.0001). mMRC grade 1 was associated with significant levels of health status impairment (SGRQ 39.4±15.5 and CAT 15.7±7.0); even patients with mMRC grade 0 had modestly elevated scores (SGRQ 28.5±15.1 and CAT 11.7±6.8). An mMRC grading ≥2 categorised 57.2% patients with low symptom (groups A and C) versus 17.2% with the CAT. Using the mMRC cut-point (≥1) resulted in similar GOLD group categorisations as the CAT (18.9%). The mMRC showed a clear relationship with health status scores; even low mMRC grades were associated with health status impairment. To really understand how AI remembers, we first have to look at how we've been testing it all this time, and why those older tests have been giving us a false sense of security. Traditionally, episodic memory in AI has been evaluated using offline benchmarks. It's basically like taking an untimed open‑book test. The book is wide open on the desk, and the AI has all the time in the world to search for the answer. The temporal distance—the time between when the AI sees the evidence and when it's actually asked the question—is rarely controlled. Ego Stream, on the other hand, introduces streaming benchmarks. It feeds the AI a continuous, dynamic stream of video, much closer to how reality actually works. The AI has to process observations incrementally, figuring out in real time what to keep and what to throw away. In the past, when we relied on exocentric video like detached bird’s‑eye security camera footage, models were judged purely on aggregate accuracy. But that creates a dangerous illusion of competence. An AI might score well overall simply because it remembers the general gist of a room while completely failing to recall fine‑grained spatial details—like exactly where you left that power bank. Those aggregate scores mask which specific forms of episodic information the model is actually degrading. Part 2, the Answer Validity Window—timing the truth. This is a huge conceptual breakthrough. In a continuous video stream, facts are inherently transient. They don’t last forever. If I ask the AI “is the glass full?” and it says yes, that answer is correct right now. But if a minute later someone drinks from it, the answer changes. That changes two parts of the conversation at once. First, it materially improves the data security and compliance posture. The broader opportunity is local AI for confidential workflows across funds and financial services.

Three years ago I moved from Russia to the UAE. A few months ago, I moved again, this time to the US. Three countries, three completely different financial and tax systems. The general principles of accounting and financial reporting are the same everywhere. The tax rules? Not even close. You can know Russian accounting cold, be the best in the room, and still land in the UAE feeling like you know nothing. I arrived just as the country was rolling out its brand-new corporate tax, a law that simply hadn’t existed before. There was no filing history to learn from, no audit track record, nobody who’d done it yet. At first, even the return itself raised a hundred questions, and the tax authority kept dropping new guidance every couple of weeks. Then there were the quirks no amount of Russian experience prepares you for. Filing deadlines here aren’t fixed. They’re different for every company. You can actually request the dates that work best for you, and more often than not, the authority says yes. It’s like that with everything: what’s taxed, what isn’t, how to calculate it, when it’s due. You learn it one piece at a time. But somewhere along the way, once you’ve put in the time and figured it out, something shifts. You stop feeling like you need to know everything, and start trusting that you can work anything out. That’s the real prize. Not the knowledge itself, but knowing how to think, how to read a system, how to take it apart and see how it actually works. That’s what I picked up over these three years, and it’s worth more than anything on my CV. And now I know it for a fact: I can figure out any system you put in front of me. They say that in this profession, the moment you stop learning, you’re already behind. To keep up, you run. To stay ahead, you run twice as fast. So here’s the next chapter: the US. One of the toughest markets out there, and a third system to learn from scratch. New studies, new rules, and a feeling that I’ll be running harder than I ever have. But this time, at least, I know what I’m walking into. And this time, I’m not doing it alone. My family is right here with me, my anchor through all of it.#InternationalTax#Finance#Accounting#CFO#ExpatLife

In 1996, I qualified for the Boston Marathon. I didn’t do it the old fashioned way - I did it by raising money for my employer at the time, a world-class cancer hospital. I was in my first job, hadn’t even entered the fundraising world yet, but I was determined to set and hit my goals: raise $4,000 and get my body - fresh from years of international development work - in shape to run 26.2 miles. The fundraising part was a great experience. People rallied around the hospital’s mission and the cutting-edge research they do. They also appreciated taking this on as a tangible commitment to the patients we served. The running part was harder. I learned to love running as an undergrad, but my usual distance was a 5K - and I ran it for good health, not to shatter records or get on a podium. But, as they say, slow and steady wins the race. In the end, I surpassed my fundraising goal and finished in 4:30. Not bad for a young woman who, a year earlier, was in the Cameroonian rain forest helping farmers integrate aquaculture into their existing practices. Fast forward thirty years. Since 1996, I’ve been blessed to work alongside amazing advancement professionals and fundraisers at a wide variety of institutions - assisting donors to make an impact and pairing their philanthropy with organizations to realize their potential. Through hard work, dedication, and a team-oriented, donor-focused approach, I’ve exceeded many a fundraising goal. As for running, that’s played out a bit differently. I’ve run off and on since 1996, but never as a daily routine. Over the past year I regained my passion and started running more regularly. It’s been a lot of work, but I set a lofty goal and sidelined the aches and pains. This past weekend, standing at the start of the Charlevoix Marathon, I’ll admit, I was nervous. Had I trained enough to physically run 26.2 again? Was I mentally ready for whatever the course would throw at me? After 5:30, I got my answers. AI doesn't fail because of technology. It fails because organizations don't trust their data. For years, cybersecurity has focused on protecting organizations from external threats. Today, a new challenge is emerging. Companies are investing millions in AI, expecting gains in productivity, faster decision-making, and measurable business outcomes. Yet many still struggle with a fundamental question: Can we trust the data behind our AI? AI can only create value when it has access to accurate, well-governed, and secure data. Without that foundation, even the most advanced models generate hesitation instead of adoption, risk instead of confidence, and costs instead of ROI. Perhaps the next competitive advantage won't come from deploying more AI. It will come from giving employees, customers, and leadership the confidence to use it at scale. In the end, the organizations that maximize the return on their AI investments won't necessarily be those with the most sophisticated models. They'll be the ones that trust their data enough to unlock AI's full potential.

# John Stewart’s Post

Founder and Managing Partner at MiddleGround Capital

8h

I've been in manufacturing for a long time and had never heard the word "destocking" before 2021. Now it's an industry buzzword that used to give me nightmares. During COVID in 2020 and 2022, industrial manufacturers bought everything they could get their hands on. Lead times had exploded. Components that used to ship in days were quoting months. If you could get material, you bought it at whatever price was available because the alternative was not being able to ship to your customers. That inventory was purchased at peak — steel at four times pre-COVID levels and energy at triple in parts of Europe. Warehouses full of the most expensive raw material possible. And then demand dropped because customers were sitting on their OWN stockpiles. They didn't need to order for months. Now you've got overpriced inventory you can't sell at a price that covers what you paid. Every shipment is a margin hit. Some of it has to be written down entirely. The operators who navigated this best were the ones who moved fastest once the signal changed. Cut the orders. Tighten the terms. Get lean before the carrying costs compound. These views reflect my personal perspective on industrial market conditions. Now and then, a company does something that reminds you what practical optimism looks like. Everyone says we need to invest in young people. Marks and Spencer has just put 1,000 paid places behind the sentence. While we argue about “lost generations”, NEET statistics and whether young people today lack resilience, opportunity or both, M&S has created 1,000 paid traineeships for 16–24 year olds across the UK and Ireland, aimed squarely at those who aren’t currently in employment, education or training. In other words, they’re not just talking about youth unemployment. They’re taking balance-sheet risk on young people who are statistically easy to overlook and practically difficult to reach. A growing number of young people in the UK now find themselves outside work, education or training, with repeated warnings that the problem could get worse if we keep treating it as an abstract social issue rather than a practical economic one. The facts, reported by BBC News and The Times, point to something bigger: this is what serious corporate citizenship looks like. It’s targeted: focused on those outside the system, not simply the already polished, connected or “high potential”. It’s paid: recognising that opportunity without income is often just privilege in better packaging. It’s scaled: 1,000 traineeships over the next 18 months isn’t a token pilot or a press-release initiative. It’s a material commitment. But more than that, it’s optimistic. It treats young people not as a social problem to be managed, but as potential to be developed. For business, that means long-term talent strategy, workforce development, social stability and customer insight wrapped into one decision. For the government, it’s a reminder that some of the most effective interventions will come from employers who can move faster than policy cycles and closer to the reality of the labour market. And for young people who’ve already been told, explicitly or implicitly, that they’ve fallen behind, it sends a very different signal: a major employer still sees them as investable. Young people don’t need another speech about aspiration from people who already had their chance. Why Strategic Simplicity Is Becoming a Competitive Advantage One of the most expensive assumptions in business is: More control = Better outcomes. So organizations add: • More reports • More approvals • More governance • More dashboards • More metrics • More systems Each addition is intended to solve a problem. Very few are ever removed. Over time, complexity becomes the operating model. After more than two decades in finance and technology transformation, I’ve noticed that organizations rarely struggle because they lack information. More often, they struggle because they are overwhelmed by it. I’ve seen organizations produce hundreds of recurring reports while leadership teams consistently relied on a small fraction of them to make decisions. I’ve seen approval processes with 7+ touchpoints where only 2 or 3 stakeholders were truly making the decision. I’ve seen project teams maintain multiple dashboards while executives continued asking for the same information in meetings. I’ve seen governance structures created to improve accountability eventually slow down the very decisions they were designed to support. ✓ More reporting doesn’t always create more insight. ✓ More approvals don’t always reduce risk. ✓ More governance doesn’t always improve accountability. ✓ More complexity doesn’t always create more control. That’s where strategic simplicity becomes powerful. Not because organizations should remove discipline. Not because controls are unnecessary. But because every process, report, approval, and governance layer should continue earning its place. Digital transformation and AI create an opportunity to ask questions many organizations avoid: → Do we still need this report? → Do we still need this approval? → Do we still need this meeting? → Do we still need this dashboard? → Do we still need this layer of governance? Because complexity is not free. It consumes time. It consumes attention. It consumes resources. And eventually, it consumes agility. The strongest organizations I’ve seen are not necessarily the most sophisticated. They are the ones that know the difference between what creates value and what simply creates complexity. Strategic simplicity is not the absence of control. It is the discipline to eliminate what no longer serves a purpose.#FinanceTransformation#DigitalTransformation#ERP#BusinessTransformation#Leadership

It is officially graduation season and time for a new generation to enter the job market. A decade ago, one of the more provocative ideas in the future‑of‑work debate was that technology would not stop at routine tasks but would transform the work of highly skilled professionals even more - as Richard and Daniel Susskind argued in The Future of the Professions. At the time, this view was an outlier in the debate because highly educated, ‘white-collar’ work was still widely seen as insulated. Today, that premise no longer feels controversial; this is especially true among the many young adults I talk with. If anything, the debate has shifted from whether professional work will change to how quickly and deeply - and what the consequences will be.

It’s easy to get caught up in moments of uncertainty – to feel anxious and unsettled about what might come next. We are certainly living in a period of conflict and change, and with that comes great uncertainty. But I prefer to see things differently: while things may not seem easy, we might just be witnessing one of the greatest opportunities of our time to build a better future. That’s one thing John Chambers, CEO of JC2 Ventures, and I discussed on the#ChambersTalks#podcast. At the heart of our conversation was the concept of the “concerned optimist,” something I’ve considered myself to be for some time. Concerned, because many people feel the pressure of a world becoming more fragmented and unpredictable. Optimistic, because today’s technologies give us the tools to solve challenges that until now would have seemed insurmountable. But technology alone is not the answer. The real question is how we choose to use it – how we lead with purpose and imagination. AI is already reshaping every industry. Yet the greatest long-term impact will not come from AI that only generates content or answers questions on a screen. It will come from AI applied in the real world. That’s where industrial AI comes in – connecting the real and digital world and turning innovation into something tangible: lower energy consumption, better use of resources, more resilient supply chains, and ultimately better outcomes for society. At Siemens, this commitment to innovation and progress is what’s shaped our own transformation journey over the years – from a broad industrial conglomerate into a focused technology company with the ambition to lead in industrial AI. And that commitment comes from our people. One thing I’ve learned over the years is that people are capable of far more than we often imagine. Leadership is not about controlling every detail. It’s about outlining a seemingly impossible dream and then empowering people – through clarity, trust and a no small amount of bravery – to figure out the details to make that dream a reality. John, thank you for the conversation – and for continuing to bring leaders together to exchange ideas and experiences. Especially in uncertain times like ours, optimism is not naïve. It is a choice to believe that we can build a better future together.

Don’t Be a Frog! On Uncertainty in the Age of AI There is no technology that is changing our working lives as quickly and as comprehensively as artificial intelligence. Nothing creates so many opportunities. That excites some people – and worries others. The fact is: uncertainties are the normal state of affairs. Every company and every individual has to deal with them. Change, adaptation and transformation are permanent tasks for organizations. This is especially true for Deutsche Telekom: When I started here almost 26 years ago, the government agency had formally already been transformed five years earlier – but it did not feel that way. The spirit of the past lived in long gray corridors, and it was customers in particular who felt it. Concerns about change are understandable. But if they get out of hand, organizations can fall victim to the “boiling frog syndrome”: The myth says that a frog that falls into a pot of hot water immediately jumps back out. But if the temperature rises only slowly, it gets used to it and stays – until it is too late. How can we prevent ourselves from becoming the frog when dealing with AI? 1️⃣ Develop a sensitive trend radar. What business models does AI make possible, how far along are others? At Telekom, we have our own teams for strategy, innovation and AI that take a very close look at this. And it is one reason why I regularly travel to Israel, China and the USA. 2️⃣ Give the right people breathing room for innovation. Anyone who is stuck in day-to-day operations all day will have little room to develop new business models. 3️⃣ Never stop learning. Of course, not every new tool is a breakthrough, not every new process a thunderclap. But only those who keep engaging with what is new have the chance to unlock the full potential of AI. 4️⃣ Hire different personalities. Teams in which many people work and think differently are more innovative. 5️⃣ Reward those on the team who take risks. A culture of learning from mistakes does not only mean allowing failure. It also means enabling others to think entrepreneurially themselves. Even in times of AI, despite all the uncertainty, what has always been true during previous major upheavals still applies: Change does not happen sometime in the future, but every day. Stay curious, stay courageous. Don’t be a frog!

After years working on MBSE in large industrial programmes, I have become convinced that the hardest problem is often not modeling the product. 𝗜𝘁 𝗶𝘀 𝘀𝘁𝗿𝘂𝗰𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗲𝗻𝗴𝗶𝗻𝗲𝗲𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘀𝘆𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗺 𝘀𝗼 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗺𝗲𝗮𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴𝗳𝘂𝗹 𝗺𝗼𝗱𝗲𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗯𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗲𝘀 𝗽𝗼𝘀𝘀𝗶𝗯𝗹𝗲. MBSE often fails not because the idea is wrong, but because the project is not yet ready for it. That was the central thesis of the talk I gave this year at the CAMPaM workshop. https://lnkd.in/ev2Wy6Aq I would like to thank Professor Hans Vangheluwe and Professor Vasco Amaral for kindly inviting me. CAMPaM has a long tradition of bringing together many of the leading researchers in MBSE, model-driven engineering, and multi-paradigm modeling for deep technical and conceptual discussions. In my previous academic life, I was lucky to take part in several editions of the workshop, so it was a real pleasure to return from an industrial perspective. The argument I presented is based on my work in MBSE and Processes, Methods & Tools across several aircraft development programmes at Airbus Defence and Space. Many organizations try to introduce MBSE into projects whose socio-technical engineering system is still too “liquid”: roles are shifting, processes are unstable, data structures are incomplete, toolchains are fragmented, and model semantics are not yet shared. In that state, MBSE can easily become frustrating — not because MBSE has no value, but because the conditions for it to create value are not yet present. My team and I have been working pragmatically on this problem: not by waiting for the perfect MBSE environment to exist, but by building tools, processes, data structures, and feedback loops that help the engineering system progressively converge. This has made me increasingly convinced that the key question is not only how to model the product, but also how to structure the socio-technical system that makes useful modeling possible. My view is that this liquid-to-solid convergence is still under-researched and insufficiently systematized. It is often reinvented from project to project, even inside the same company. Understanding this transition better could significantly improve the return on investment of MBSE initiatives and strengthen industrial competitiveness. Psychische Gesundheit ist eine gesellschaftliche Aufgabe. Am Mittwoch hatte ich die Gelegenheit, an der 41. Bertha-Benz-Vorlesung der Daimler und Benz Stiftung teilzunehmen. Das Thema: „Depressionen in Zeiten großer Veränderungen“ mit Prof. Dr. Eva-Lotta Brakemeier von der Universität Greifswald. Die aktuellen Herausforderungen sind enorm. Geopolitische Konflikte, die Transformation unserer Industrie, Digitalisierung, Klimawandel und gesellschaftliche Polarisierung. Viele Menschen erleben diese Entwicklungen als Belastung, verbunden mit Unsicherheit und zunehmendem Druck. Umso wichtiger ist es, offen über psychische Gesundheit zu sprechen. Depressionen sind keine Frage von Stärke oder Schwäche. Sie entstehen aus einem komplexen Zusammenspiel vieler Faktoren und sie betreffen Menschen in allen Bereichen unserer Gesellschaft. Entscheidend sind dabei soziale Beziehungen, Zusammenhalt und das Gefühl, nicht allein zu sein. Auch in der Arbeitswelt trägt jeder Verantwortung. Gute Arbeitsbedingungen, Mitbestimmung, gegenseitiger Respekt und ein wertschätzendes Miteinander sind nicht nur wichtige Voraussetzungen für wirtschaftlichen Erfolg, sondern auch für die Gesundheit der Beschäftigten. Wer Veränderungsprozesse gemeinsam gestaltet und Menschen beteiligt, schafft Vertrauen und stärkt die Resilienz in schwierigen Zeiten. Die Vorlesung hat einmal gezeigt: Psychische Gesundheit ist kein individuelles Randthema, sondern eine gesamtgesellschaftliche Aufgabe. Gerade in Zeiten großer Umbrüche brauchen wir Solidarität, Zusammenhalt und die Bereitschaft, füreinander da zu sein. Mein Dank gilt der Daimler und Benz Stiftung für die Organisation dieser wichtigen Veranstaltung und für den Impuls, ein Thema in den Mittelpunkt zu stellen, das uns alle betrifft.

Most brands spend months building a training program for a new location, then wonder why the team falls apart in week two. Here's what actually happens on the ground: the team is overwhelmed, retention drops under pressure, and the volume of information they received before opening becomes noise the moment their first real rush hits. Traditional training models weren't built for opening conditions. They're front-loaded, designed for a classroom pace, and assume people can absorb and apply everything at once. That's not how humans work and it's definitely not how a new store operates. I've been rebuilding how we approach openings. Not more training. Better-timed training. That means sequencing content around what the team actually needs in the first 30 days. It means simplifying ruthlessly by identifying the five to eight critical behaviors that drive performance and making sure those land before anything else. It means putting the right information in front of people at the moment they can actually use it, not three weeks before doors open. If you're scaling a multi-unit brand and your new locations are slow to ramp, the problem usually isn't effort. It's architecture. Rethink the sequence before you add more content. Rethink the timing before you add more hours. Build for the pace of opening week, not the pace of a training room. Ramp success isn't something you hope for. It's something you design.#MultiUnit#TrainingAndDevelopment#OperationalExcellence
