June at Beiersdorf is Development Month. Development Month is Beiersdorf Group’s global initiative dedicated to giving every employee the time, space and inspiration to engage with their own development, in a way that feels meaningful to them. This year’s theme is Make it Personal, which really resonated with me. As a leader, one of the things I am most passionate about is helping people be more intentional about their growth. Not in a rigid “five-year-plan-written-in-stone” kind of way, because let’s be honest, careers rarely follow a perfectly straight line. Passion areas evolve. Opportunities appear. Priorities shift. The act of pausing and asking yourself: What do I want my career to become? What kind of work gives me energy? Where are my strengths? What do I need to build next? What support do I need from my manager? That reflection is powerful. It also gives managers a much clearer view of how to create the right opportunities for people to develop, stretch and shine. I’ve been working with my team on a simple Career Development Plan template to help bring this thinking to life. It covers career aspirations, energising and draining work, strengths, growth areas, skills to build, action plans and manager notes. Development should feel personal, practical and owned by the individual, not like another form to complete before a performance conversation. I hope this template is useful for anyone wanting to be more intentional about their own development, or wanting to support their team’s growth more meaningfully. French-based engineering and technology company, Technip Energies has secured a major engineering, procurement, construction, installation and commissioning (EPCIC) contract for the Coral Norte floating liquefied natural gas (FLNG) project offshore Mozambique. The French energy services company announced that the award, together with previously disclosed contracts linked to the development, represents a major project valued at more than €1 billion ($1.14 billion) in revenue. The project will be executed in partnership with JGC Holdings Corporation and Samsung Heavy Industries on behalf of Mozambique Rovuma Venture SpA. Mozambique Rovuma Venture is jointly owned by Eni and several international partners, including China National Petroleum Corporation(CNPC), Empresa Nacional de Hidrocarbonetos EP, XRG and Korea Gas Corporation(KOGAS). Predicting how single cells respond to drugs faces two obstacles. Single-cell RNA sequencing destroys each cell it measures, so treated and untreated cells cannot be matched one to one, and responses must be compared as distributions rather than as paired cells. Separately, most methods cannot predict the response to a drug absent from the training data, the setting that matters most for drug discovery. Optimal transport can map one cell-state distribution onto another, and methods such as CellOT have applied it to perturbation modelling. These solvers are unconditional: each drug or dose needs its own model, so none can generalize to a new condition. Driessen et al., in Nature Machine Intelligence, introduce the Conditional Monge Gap (CMonge), which conditions a single transport map on arbitrary covariates. 🧬 Key results 1️⃣ A single conditional map instead of per-condition models: CMonge builds on the Monge Gap to learn one global transport map conditioned on drug, dose, or their combinations, rather than fitting a separate model for each condition. Learning the map directly avoids the training instability of input-convex neural network solvers. 2️⃣ One model performs comparably to per-condition models: On the SciPlex3 dataset of three human cancer cell lines, a single CMonge model conditioned on drug and dose performed comparably to condition-specific models trained one per drug–dose pair. The strongest dose, 10,000 nM, was the hardest to predict. 3️⃣ Unseen drugs predicted from chemical structure alone: On the full SciPlex panel of 187 drugs, holding out nine drugs at a time, CMonge generalized to unseen drugs using only RDKit molecular fingerprints. It outperformed chemCPA at the strongest dose (R² 0.78 versus 0.76), with a wider margin on metrics that capture distributional heterogeneity. 4️⃣ Heterogeneity captured at a fraction of the parameters: chemCPA tends to capture the average response, often producing collapsed predictions, whereas CMonge preserves the spread and heterogeneity of perturbed cells (MMD 0.020 versus 0.195). CMonge uses 23,000 to 580,000 parameters, against roughly 1.37 million for chemCPA and over 100 million for single-cell foundation models. The formulation is independent of the condition type, so it could incorporate covariates such as cell type or time; the authors report a parallel application to CAR-T cell designs. They note open challenges including new cell types, out-of-distribution conditions, and robustness

- Denunciar esta publicação

O avanço dos pagamentos digitais exige um novo compromisso com a segurança Por: Renato Wada, IT Security Director da Global Payments. Os pagamentos digitais deixaram de ser uma tendência para se tornar infraestrutura crítica. E, como toda infraestrutura essencial, sua confiabilidade passou a ser inegociável. Em 2025, mais da metade das compras realizadas globalmente no e-commerce passou por carteiras digitais. Pix, pagamentos por aproximação e transações em tempo real transformaram o que antes era inovação em expectativa básica. Mas existe uma equação inevitável nesse cenário: o setor que conquistou a confiança de bilhões de consumidores agora precisa mantê-la. Segundo o Global Payments Report 2026, estudo desenvolvido pela Worldpay, agora Global Payments, e que analisou o comportamento do setor de meios de pagamentos em 42 países do mundo, durante o ano de 2025, as carteiras digitais já representaram 56% do valor transacionado no e-commerce global e 33% nos pontos de venda físicos, enquanto os cartões representaram 48% das transações presenciais e 33% do e-commerce. Esses números confirmam não apenas o avanço acelerado da digitalização, mas também a crescente complexidade do ecossistema de pagamentos. Essa evolução é impulsionada pela busca de conveniência, velocidade e fluidez. Consumidores esperam concluir transações em segundos, independentemente do canal. Para as empresas, essa dinâmica abre oportunidades relevantes de crescimento, mas traz, na mesma proporção, uma responsabilidade crítica: preservar a confiança que sustenta esse sistema. One thing I've learned over the years is that culture is usually easier to recognise than it is to define. You see it in small moments. How people react when things go wrong. Whether colleagues help each other without being asked. Whether someone feels comfortable suggesting a new idea. Or, in this case, whether twelve people decide to spend time preparing for a marathon together. Reading about Epson's first team at the Riga Marathon made me smile because it felt like one of those moments. Not because of the running itself, but because of what sits behind it — initiative, encouragement, commitment, and a sense of belonging. Those qualities matter on a marathon course, and they matter in business too. Thank you to everyone who represented Epson in Riga. More importantly, thank you for reminding us that culture is something people create together every day.

Epson Deutschland GmbH Tech Day at the Epson Experience Center in Neuss 🤩 As part of the Japan Desk at The Office of Economic Development Düsseldorf, in order to provide the best possible support to Japanese companies in the EU’s largest Japanese business hub, I naturally seize every opportunity to engage with them and learn about their business activities and technological innovations (definitely one of the many benefits of our work)💡 So, when Antje Kleine-Horst kindly invited me to the Epson Tech Day on 11 June when we met at the opening of the Epson Experience Centre in April, I didn’t have to think twice 🙏 At the Experience Centre, visitors can learn first-hand about Epson’s innovative solutions in fields such as commercial printing, industrial manufacturing, robotics and automation through real-world application scenarios, guided by experts and supported by hands-on demonstrations, and experience them for themselves 🖨️🏷️🤖 The Experience Center is not only another fine example of the innovative strength of a Japanese company based in Düsseldorf, but also demonstrates that Japanese companies’ investments in the region extend beyond the city limits - like Epson, numerous companies based in Düsseldorf have invested in the surrounding area, and vice versa 📈🇯🇵 In addition to a series of insightful presentations by customers and partner companies during Epson Tech Day on topics such as the automation of manufacturing processes, machine vision, and virtual simulation models, I personally found Ekkehart Padberg’s presentation on change management particularly inspiring: Change - whether in automation processes, organizational structures, or society - must always be conceived from a human perspective and implemented collaboratively, because change can only succeed if it fosters a sense of belonging and is associated by the group with added value. Otherwise, there is a risk of reflexively clinging to the “tried and true” or, at worst, idealizing a past that never actually existed 🔄 Thank you so much for letting me take part in this exciting event, and I am already looking forward to my next visit to the Epson Experience Center 😃#Epson#EpsonExperienceCenter#TechDay#Automation#Robotics#Manufacturing

While we chase an “intelligence system” on the frontier, in the “heartland” we scratch our heads. Power and human dynamics becoming the ultimate cover for “do now, ask for forgiveness later.” 1. Anthropic gets put on time out. For whatever reason, their capabilities are concerning enough to warrant government intervention. Logic - new model is too powerful, shut it down. But what is the gap between what it can do and other competitors? Clearly, anthropic has capabilities others don’t? 2. Are their Competitors (OpenAI, SpaceX, Google, Amazon, etc) capable of reaching Anthropic’s capabilities? Whatever the gap in capabilities to get to “time out, too powerful”, is closing. 3. There is no obvious permanent moat that keeps Anthropic uniquely ahead. Safe to say, although there is a difference in capabilties today, the gap will close. 4. Governments increasingly view frontier AI as a strategic asset. But they only put Anthropic in jail… but why not the other companies? 5. Even if we create regulations and policy to attempt to “constrain” what corps are allowed to do or not with these models, regulators don’t have the capabilities to audit, understand, inspect, or control the underlying systems anyway. After sharing a bunch of Unit27 projects one at a time, I’m aware they can look a little scattered from the outside. Textile compliance. Worker attestation. Movement analysis. Music performance. Compute flexibility. Disaster recovery evidence. Agent authority. AI workflow exceptions. Field-practice decisions. Admittedly, this is not the world’s cleanest LinkedIn category. So now the public archive has a map! The connection I keep coming back to is structural intelligence, and I mean that in a practical sense. Most of these projects start with the same kind of failure: a decision, record, or claim gets separated from the context that would make it reviewable later. A garment loses its provenance. A worker contribution disappears before it can travel with the product record. A tool changes what movement data means. A musical gesture disappears once the performance is over. A flexibility promise gets separated from the operating conditions and settlement context behind it. A recovery packet gets separated from the human review behind it. An autonomous agent reaches settlement without live proof that its authority still holds. An AI exception gets smoothed into a final outcome without preserving what happened in between. A field-practice call gets made after the plan, the conditions, and the group context have drifted apart. Unit27 is where I’ve been building systems for those moments. The goal is to give the decision, record, or workflow enough structure that someone else can look back at it later and still understand what mattered and the logic beneath that decision, record, or workflow.#Unit27#StructuralIntelligence

Here’s some of what I shared: - Seize every opportunity and never look back. - When you find people you admire, study them. - If you have a team sport mentality, you can move an organization forward. - Reward not just results, but the way they’re achieved. - Be open about mistakes. - Make work fun—it makes us better people. - Denunciar esta publicación

La transformación de la atención cardiovascular no depende únicamente de nuevos tratamientos. Depende, sobre todo, de cómo somos capaces de organizar el sistema alrededor del paciente. Nos alegra ver la puesta en marcha de EVA Bridge, una iniciativa impulsada por Daiichi Sankyo España que cuenta con el aval de la SECA Sociedad Española de Calidad Asistencial(SECA), SEDISA - Sociedad Española de Directivos de la Salud(SEDISA) para reforzar la coordinación entre Cardiología y Atención Primaria en el seguimiento de pacientes postinfarto. Desde Pëtri hemos tenido el privilegio de participar en el diseño y desarrollo estratégico de este proyecto, trabajando codo a codo con el equipazo de Daiichi, Ariana López Cuartero y Guillermo Pintor Felez junto a profesionales clínicos, gestores y equipos multidisciplinares para construir un modelo asistencial que facilite una transición más segura, coordinada y eficiente entre niveles asistenciales. EVA Bridge aborda algunos de los grandes retos que encontramos hoy en los sistemas sanitarios: • Mejorar la continuidad asistencial. • Reducir la variabilidad clínica. • Incorporar herramientas digitales para el seguimiento. • Potenciar el papel activo del paciente. • Medir resultados y generar aprendizaje continuo. Creemos que los verdaderos cambios en salud ocurren cuando se combinan evidencia clínica, liderazgo organizativo y diseño de procesos centrados en las personas. Gracias a todos los profesionales y organizaciones que han contribuido a hacer posible este proyecto que tiene mucho camino por delante. Enhorabuena equipazo!!! Inés Domínguez Fernández Felipe Iglesias Pernas Seguimos…..

1983 seguidores

2 semanas

Las mejores iniciativas en salud no nacen de una organización. Nacen de la colaboración: ➡️ De profesionales que comparten conocimiento. ➡️ De instituciones que alinean esfuerzos. ➡️ Y de una visión común: mejorar la vida de los pacientes. Nos enorgullece haber acompañado a Daiichi Sankyo España a impulsar este espacio de trabajo y reflexión para avanzar hacia una atención postinfarto más coordinada y efectiva. En EVA Bridge, expertos clínicos, gestores sanitarios y profesionales del ámbito asistencial han trabajado conjuntamente para identificar oportunidades de mejora en la coordinación entre niveles asistenciales, un aspecto clave para garantizar la continuidad de la atención tras un infarto. El resultado es una hoja de ruta orientada a reducir barreras, optimizar procesos y favorecer un seguimiento más integrado de los pacientes a lo largo de todo su recorrido asistencial.

Google just asked the markets for $80 billion. Not because it's short of cash — Alphabet generated ~$174B in operating cash flow over the last year. So why raise at all? Here's the part the headlines miss: this is a choice of equity over more debt. Over the past year Alphabet raised $85B+ in debt, pushing total debt above $100B. Long-term debt sat quietly around $11–13B for years — then jumped to $46.5B in 2025 and $77.5B by March 2026. Stacking another $80B of borrowing on top of that would strain the balance sheet and risk pressure on its credit rating. So Alphabet is reaching for equity instead: → $30B underwritten offering → $40B at-the-market program → $10B private placement bought directly by Berkshire Hathaway Yes, new shares mean dilution. Worth a read from MIT IDE on where agentic commerce actually stands today. The piece pulls together the protocol work like MCP, A2A, and AP2 alongside the payment alliances forming around it. The part that stuck with me is a simpler question, which is who the shopping agent actually works for. As they frame it in the article, the "bowling-shoe" agent is built and run by the retailer or platform. It is easy to use and optimized for that environment, but you do not own it, and the incentive is to design it around the seller's goals. A "bring-your-own" agent flips that dynamic. It is configured around your preferences and travels with you across stores, though it carries its own setup and compatibility tradeoffs. That distinction matters more than it first appears. Bob Hedges makes the point that the tempting economics of advertising and product placement could quietly erode an agent's objectivity, and that there is little incentive today for platforms to disclose what is driving a recommendation. The trust gap is real. The Visa report cited in the piece found that 79 percent of consumers who are already interested in AI commerce still have data privacy concerns. None of this has been settled yet. The liability rules, the business models, and the question of whether people will pay directly for advice they can trust are all still open. The choice the article closes on is the one I will be watching, which is whether platforms decide to serve consumers or to monetize them.

While exploring Coca-Cola's iconic campaigns, I found myself looking at two campaigns that are more than 50 years apart: "I'd Like to Buy the World a Coke" (1971) and the recently relaunched "Share a Coke" (2025). At first, they felt completely different. The Hilltop campaign brought people together through one powerful, collective message. It imagined a world connected by a shared experience. The 2025 version of Share a Coke takes a very different approach. Instead of telling one story, it invites millions of people to tell their own. Through personalized bottles, digital interactions, and user-generated content, the audience is no longer just watching the campaign, they're becoming a part of it. That contrast is what caught my attention. The execution has evolved with every generation, but the core idea hasn't. Coca-Cola has never just marketed a beverage. It has consistently built campaigns around human connection. The medium changes. The way people participate changes. But the emotion at the centre stays the same. That observation made me think about how I would reimagine the original Hilltop campaign today. I would call it "Back to the Table." The idea is simple: reconnect with someone who has been part of your journey- a school friend, an old teammate, a cousin, or a college roommate. Meet over a Coke and a meal. Share one memory that still makes you smile, and one story about how both of you have changed since then. Record that conversation and share it, creating thousands of authentic stories instead of one scripted film. To me, that's the natural evolution of Hilltop. The original campaign imagined people coming together. Today, we have the opportunity to help people reconnect in real life and let those moments become the campaign itself. That's what I admire most about Coca-Cola's marketing journey. Across decades, platforms, and generations, the brand has adapted the way it tells stories without changing the emotion those stories are built on. And maybe that's what makes iconic marketing truly timeless. Theme 2: Iconic Marketing#CokeAmbassador

One unexpected side effect of AI: I have never had so many product ideas. And I have never abandoned so many of them. A few years ago, turning an idea into a PRD, workflow, wireframe, or implementation plan took a lot of effort. Today, I can sit with an AI for an hour and walk away with a refined problem statement, user personas, workflows, feature lists, edge cases and a detailed PRD The barrier to ideation has collapsed. Which sounds great. Until you open the project folder and realize half of those ideas are still sitting there. Unbuilt. What I have learned is that AI dramatically reduces the cost of thinking about products. It doesn't reduce the cost of committing to one. The hard part is still deciding: - Is this problem worth solving? - Am I willing to spend weeks or months on it? - What am I saying "no" to by saying "yes" to this? In hindsight, most of my learning has come not from the PRDs I have written, but from the products I actually built. Because reality introduces constraints that no brainstorming session can simulate. How are you filtering the noise? How do you decide which AI-generated spec actually deserves your time?#BuildinginPublic#ProductThinking#BuildingwithAI

It is officially graduation season and time for a new generation to enter the job market. Many of these young adults have impressive CVs with strong grades from great universities, extracurricular activities, and relevant internships under their belts - certainly not how my CV looked at age 23! It is said that the hardest job to land is your first one. My colleague, Sára Juřenová and I have been diving into the latest research surrounding entry-level work. Data show that youth unemployment still moves largely with macroeconomic forces such as interest rates and inflation - the U.S. unemployment rate for 20-24 year olds is actually nearly 1.5% pt lower today than when ChatGPT was first launched. The impact of AI is showing up in a different way. AI is quietly reshaping entry-level jobs by absorbing many of the tasks that once gave graduates their start. A decade ago, one of the more provocative ideas in the future‑of‑work debate was that technology would not stop at routine tasks but would transform the work of highly skilled professionals even more - as Richard and Daniel Susskind argued in The Future of the Professions. At the time, this view was an outlier in the debate because highly educated, ‘white-collar’ work was still widely seen as insulated. Today, that premise no longer feels controversial; this is especially true among the many young adults I talk with. If anything, the debate has shifted from whether professional work will change to how quickly and deeply - and what the consequences will be.

A Microsoft lawyer said one sentence under oath last June that now anchors half of Europe's AI policy. Asked whether French citizens' data on Microsoft's European servers could ever reach US authorities without consent, he answered that he could not guarantee it. The sentence is true. The lesson most of Europe drew from it is wrong, and it is costing us the future. The conclusion everyone reached was simple: stop using American AI. But the dependency did not arrive with AI. It arrived with SharePoint, with Databricks running on Azure and AWS, with the entire stack we signed off years ago. Banning the newest and most valuable layer while keeping everything underneath is not sovereignty. It is self-handicapping with a noble name. Sovereignty is not a shield you request from Brussels. It is the spoils of those who fought and won. Winning today means using the best tools, the American ones included, while building the layers that hold your knowledge, data, orchestration, memory, so the model on top stays replaceable. Competence compounds. The company that trains two hundred people on real agent workflows today builds a lead a competitor cannot buy later. Whoever waits has already chosen to fall behind.

Construction update from Germany. At our offshore wind project Nordseecluster A, the inter-array cable campaign is finished: 48 cables laid, buried and terminated, and tested, through some of the toughest offshore weather of the year. Cables rarely draw the attention that foundations, substations, or turbines do. Yet this package – laying, burial, termination, testing – is one of the most coordination-intensive scopes of any offshore wind farm: four vessels, more than 200 people, parallel works running across the site every day. With the array connected, Phase A has now moved on to turbine installation. The first of 44 Vestas turbines went in last week, with all 660 MW for NSC A on track for commissioning in early 2027. Together, Nordseecluster A and B will deliver around 6.5 TWh of clean electricity a year – domestic, scalable energy that does not depend on imported fuel or geopolitical conditions. Kudos to our#TeamRWE IAC and OSS teams, whose joint work kept the grid connection with TenneT on track, and to our project partner Norges Bank Investment Management.
